ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, directors, officers and foreign corporate shareholders against Canadian sanctions lists (Special Economic Measures Act and Regulations, United Nations Act Regulations), OFAC SDN list, UN Security Council Consolidated List, EU and UK consolidated financial sanctions lists; enhanced due diligence under PCMLTFA and FINTRAC Guidance for politically exposed persons (domestic and foreign); ongoing adverse-media screening and sanctions re-screening at least every 90 days.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (British Columbia Corporate Registry)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must be in English or French and use Latin script. The name must be distinctive and not confusingly similar to existing BC corporate names, trademarks or business names. Foreign names must be transliterated into Latin alphabet. The corporate name of an unlimited liability company must include 'Unlimited Liability Company' or 'ULC' or a corresponding French equivalent, such as 'Compagnie à responsabilité illimitée'.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection, the applicant may file a written administrative appeal to the Registrar of Companies under the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, within 30 days of the notice of rejection. The appeal must set out the grounds of confusion or distinctiveness, provide supporting trademark or trade-name evidence, and pay the prescribed statutory appeal fee. An extension of a name reservation may be requested before expiry by filing an extension request through BC Corporate Online and paying the applicable fee; extensions are generally granted once for an additional 56-day period.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office with a physical street address in British Columbia is permissible for administrative and licensing operations; however, the registered office must have an actual physical address within BC where legal notices may be served. A purely virtual or mail-only address without a physical presence is not permissible as a registered office.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (approximately 2% annual probability) for this low-risk digital audio licensing business, absent any AML/CFT trigger, complaint, or FINTRAC risk assessment indicating artificial substance.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57 (British Columbia), ss. 1(1) (unlimited liability company definition), 10–12 (incorporation), 24–25 (name requirements), 51.1–51.9 (ULC-specific provisions); Company Act transitional provisions do not apply to BC ULCs incorporated after 2004
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Corporate Registry, BC Ministry of Finance – Registrar of Companies, Victoria, British Columbia
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Incorporation Application (Form 1), Notice of Articles (Form 2), and required ULC Memorandum adopting the Business Corporations Act model; Certificate of Incorporation issued on registration
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital for a BC ULC; shares may be issued with nil or nominal consideration without escrow or capitalization deposit requirements, subject only to the solvency-based declaration of each subscriber
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the incorporation of the Company under the Business Corporations Act (British Columbia) is approved, together with its Notice of Articles and ULC Memorandum. FURTHER RESOLVED, that the subscriber shareholders subscribe to the issued no-par common shares set out in the share subscription ledger, such shares being fully paid upon delivery of this resolution. FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Registered and Records Office shall be at [address, City, BC] and that [name] is appointed sole director. FURTHER RESOLVED, that [name] as President, [name] as Secretary, and [name] as Chief Financial Officer are appointed officers with authority to open bank accounts and execute all documents for the corporate business.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registries Online Portal (Corporate Registry, Victoria, BC)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Initiate a NUANS name search through the BC Registries online platform selecting 'BC Unlimited Liability Company' as the legal element; the proposed name must end with 'Unlimited Liability Company' or the abbreviation 'ULC'. Submit the name reservation request electronically, pay the prescribed fee, and preserve the reservation for 56 days. Record the corporate name approval number for use in Form 1.
required_dossiers: NUANS Name Search Request for BC ULC
Proposed corporate name and jurisdiction of records
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected for confusion or prohibited language, file a revised name reservation application within the statutory response window or submit a written objection to the Registrar of Companies for administrative review; no additional period is granted beyond the 56-day reservation validity unless renewed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of Incorporation Application, Notice of Articles, and ULC Memorandum
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registrar of Companies (BC Registries Online, Corporate Registry, Victoria)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare and file the Incorporation Application (Form 1), Notice of Articles (Form 2), and ULC Memorandum setting out unlimited liability of members. Include registered office address, director names and residential addresses, share structure, and the approved name reservation number. Upon filing and payment of the statutory fee, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation and the company comes into existence.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried or rejected, correct deficiencies and file an amended Notice of Articles within the Registrar's stated deadline; where errors post-date incorporation, apply for voluntary correction under the BCBCA with an affidavit explaining the defect and pay the prescribed amendment fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Organization – First Board Resolution, Share Issuance, and Officer Appointments
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the Company; Registrar of Companies for registered-office records
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first board meeting or adopt the written first board resolution to approve the share subscription ledger, allot shares to founding shareholders, designate the BC Registered and Records Office, and appoint officers (President, Secretary, Chief Financial Officer). Prepare and maintain the corporate minute book, share certificates, register of directors, and register of shareholders at the registered office.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If an officer or director refuses to act, the board may pass a subsequent resolution to fill the vacancy and file an updated Notice of Directors with the Registrar; omitted minutes may be ratified by unanimous consent resolution at the next meeting.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Federal Business Number, GST/HST, and Payroll Account Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Registration Online (BRO)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register the company for a federal Business Number (BN) immediately after incorporation, opening a GST/HST account (5% GST; BC PST is separately administered by the Province), and a payroll deductions account if employees are hired. For royalty-free stock music subscription sales to Canadian customers, GST/HST applies to taxable digital supplies; export sales to non-residents are generally zero-rated.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CRA queries the registration, respond through My Business Account by attaching corrected Articles and a director authorization letter; retroactive account adjustments may be requested by a formal notice of objection.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: City of Vancouver (or applicable BC municipal) Business Licence Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Where the company maintains an office in Vancouver, file the Business Licence Application under the classification 'Digital Media / Online Services – Audio Licensing', stating the ULC corporate name, registered office, and intended commercial activity of licensing royalty-free stock music subscriptions. Obtain zoning confirmation for office use and pay the annual licence fee based on number of employees.
required_dossiers: Completed City of Vancouver Business Licence Application
Registered office lease or occupancy proof
Criminal record check for applicants (if applicable)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is refused for zoning or classification reasons, submit a revised application re-classifying the use as 'remote digital marketplace' to the Business Licence Inspector, or appeal to the City of Vancouver Property Use Inspection and Licensing Board within the stated appeal period.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: WorkSafeBC Employer Registration and Occupational Health and Safety Clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: WorkSafeBC (Workers' Compensation Board of British Columbia)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register the company as an employer with WorkSafeBC, provide estimated payroll by occupation, and obtain a clearance letter confirming coverage. Implement a written injury-prevention program for office-based staff, including ergonomic furniture, emergency response, and first-aid requirements under the Workers Compensation Act.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If registration is delayed or assessments are disputed, file an adjusted payroll statement and request a review by WorkSafeBC; unresolved disputes may proceed to the Review Division within 45 days of the assessment.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Environmental Exemption Confirmation and Sectoral Compliance Notice
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy; Environmental Assessment Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Confirm that the digital audio licensing operation is an office-based service with no physical manufacturing footprint and therefore outside the prescribed reviewable project classes under the Environmental Assessment Act, SBC 2018, c. 51. Where the office disposes of electronic waste, register the company as a 'producer' or document compliance with the BC Recycling Regulation (B.C. Reg. 449/2004), and align with municipal wastewater discharge rules.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Ministry of Environment issues a compliance inquiry, submit an environmental impact assessment confirmation letter and waste manifest; if a reviewable project classification is nonetheless triggered, file an application for an exemption order with supporting technical data.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: City of Vancouver Business Licence Office (municipal licensing); Consumer Protection BC (registration for consumer-facing digital commerce, low risk tier); SOCAN/Re:Sound membership voluntary for royalty-free original catalogue, not a statutory license
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Municipal Business Licence – Digital Media / Online Audio Licensing; no separate provincial industry permit required for royalty-free stock music distribution

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy – Environmental Assessment Office
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt – Office-Based Digital Service; no Environmental Assessment Certificate required under the Environmental Assessment Act, SBC 2018, c. 51; Class of operation: Schedule 1 excluded (non-industrial, zero-emission, remote service delivery)
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater: indirect sanitary discharge to municipal sewer compliant with the Metro Vancouver Sewer Use Bylaw (no industrial process effluent); Emissions: no VOC or particulate release from server-based operations, data-centre hosting subject to landlord utility compliance; Waste: electronic and battery waste managed under the BC Recycling Regulation (B.C. Reg. 449/2004); office solid waste under municipal curbside programs

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification under the BC Fire Code and local fire inspector sign-off (portable fire extinguishers, emergency exit signage, fire drill records); structural load inspection for office occupancy under the BC Building Code (maximum persons per floor); electrical safety clearance for office and rack-mounted audio equipment; WorkSafeBC occupational health and safety clearance (injury prevention program, first-aid kit, ergonomic workstations)

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) — federal corporate income tax under Part I of the Income Tax Act, GST/HST under the Excise Tax Act, and payroll source deductions; primary digital portal is CRA 'My Business Account' (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/e-services-businesses/business-account.html) and Business Registration Online for new accounts. British Columbia corporate income tax is assessed and collected by the CRA under the federal-provincial tax collection agreement, while the B.C. Ministry of Finance / Consumer Taxation Branch separately administers the 7% Provincial Sales Tax (PST) through the eTaxBC portal. The BC ULC must also maintain active corporate registry status with the BC Corporate Registry (OneStop / Corporate Online).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For a foreign-owned BC Unlimited Liability Company (ULC): (1) incorporate under the British Columbia Business Corporations Act via BC Corporate Online/OneStop; the incorporation certificate issues a BC corporate registration number; (2) obtain a 9-digit CRA Business Number (BN) by registering through Business Registration Online or by submitting Form RC1 to CRA; the BN forms the base for the federal corporation income tax account (RC0001); (3) register for GST/HST (same BN, RT account) — mandatory once the CAD 30,000 small-supplier threshold is exceeded or when the ULC needs to claim input tax credits and zero-rating for exports; (4) register with the BC Ministry of Finance for a PST vendor account before any taxable retail sale of tangible personal property or specified taxable service in BC (digital music subscriptions are generally outside PST, but physical media shipments into BC are taxable); (5) if the ULC employs Canadian personnel, open a CRA payroll deductions account and a BC Employer Health Tax account; (6) if physical media is imported or exported, open a CRA RM import/export account for customs purposes; non-resident shareholders may appoint Canadian legal counsel and must ensure the registered and records office in BC is maintained.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation (Canadian) / Pass_Through_Eligible (U.S. check-the-box). For Canadian Income Tax Act purposes, a BC ULC is a corporation resident in Canada and is taxed at the entity level on worldwide income; it is not a Canadian-controlled private corporation if controlled by non-residents, and therefore the combined federal plus BC general corporate income tax rate applies (federal 15% + BC 12% = 27%) with no small business deduction. For U.S. federal tax purposes, the BC ULC is generally eligible for pass-through classification by filing Form 8832 (check-the-box), enabling treatment as a disregarded entity or partnership; territorial scope and tax-exempt zone treatment are not applicable because Canada taxes resident corporations on worldwide income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Available elections and mechanisms: (a) U.S. check-the-box election under Treas. Reg. sections 301.7701-1 through -3 using Form 8832 to classify the ULC as a disregarded entity or partnership for U.S. tax purposes; (b) voluntary GST/HST registration election under section 240(1) of the Excise Tax Act, permitting a small supplier to register voluntarily and claim input tax credits and export zero-rating refunds; (c) Canada-U.S. Tax Convention (Fifth Protocol) Article IV(7) fiscally transparent entity rule, which supports the look-through treatment of income derived by U.S. resident owners through a Canadian ULC for treaty withholding purposes; (d) NR301/NR302 treaty-based withholding reduction certification for cross-border distributions to non-resident shareholders; (e) hybrid mismatch rules under the Income Tax Act (effective for payments after July 1, 2022) generally operate by mandatory deduction disallowance rather than by election, and the ULC must maintain transfer pricing and economic substance contemporaneous documentation to avoid hybrid mismatch adjustments.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_filing_calendar_summary: Calendar year: corporate income tax returns (T2) due six months after fiscal year-end; GST/HST returns due monthly, quarterly, or annually depending on revenue (annual filers by three months after fiscal year-end); GST/HST instalments apply only to large businesses; T4/T4A payroll information due by end of February; T106/TP106 information returns for reportable cross-border transactions; Form 8832 U.S. election due within 75 days of entity formation or as a late election with penalty relief if within 3 years and 75 days.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.penalty_regime_for_non_registration: Failure to register for GST/HST when required triggers assessment of net tax, arrears interest, and penalties under sections 280 and 285 of the Excise Tax Act; failure to file a T2 return attracts penalties under section 162 of the Income Tax Act, including an initial 5% penalty plus 1% per month up to 12 months, repeated failure penalties, and gross-negligence penalties under section 163(2) equal to 50% of understated tax.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_authority_contacts: CRA International and Large Business Directorate for non-resident matters; BC Ministry of Finance, Consumer Taxation Branch, Victoria BC for PST; Canada Border Services Agency for customs export declarations; U.S. IRS via Publication 519 / competent authority under Article XXVI of the Canada-U.S. Convention.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.registration_status_check: A ULC may verify its BN and account registration status by accessing CRA 'My Business Account'; BC PST registration is verifiable through eTaxBC; federal corporate status is verifiable through Corporations Canada Online Filing Centre and BC Corporate Registry.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) at 5%, a value-added tax administered by the CRA, plus British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST) at 7%, a retail sales tax administered by the B.C. Ministry of Finance; British Columbia does not participate in the Harmonized Sales Tax (HST). Digital stock-music licenses, royalties, and audio subscription fees are taxable supplies of intangible personal property under GST; BC PST generally exempts digital audio downloads and subscription streaming but applies to physical media such as CDs and USB drives sold for use in BC.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: GST/HST small supplier threshold: CAD 30,000 of worldwide taxable supplies in the current calendar quarter or in the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters (Excise Tax Act). For non-resident digital suppliers of audio/music services, registration is required once taxable supplies to Canadian resident customers exceed CAD 30,000 in a 12-month period under the July 1, 2021 cross-border e-commerce rules; since the ULC will be a Canadian resident corporation, registration is mandatory immediately from first taxable supply. BC PST has no registration threshold: a PST vendor permit is required before making any taxable sale of tangible personal property or specified taxable service in BC, and PST of 7% applies regardless of volume.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: None. Canada does not operate a mandatory real-time fiscal clearance system, does not require API-based invoice clearance, and does not impose digital stamping or tax-authority invoice pre-approval. The CRA accepts electronic invoices and records if they are legible, complete, and retained in a readable format. A voluntary Pan-Canadian PEPPOL interoperable e-invoicing framework is available for B2G and B2B exchange (supported by Shared Services Canada / Treasury Board Secretariat), but it is not a statutory mandate. For an ISIC 5920 royalty-free stock music marketplace, the ULC may generate invoices through Stripe or PayPal provided each taxable invoice contains the supplier BN, date, customer name, description of the licensed audio rights, GST/HST amount or zero-rating basis, and the foreign customer jurisdiction for export zero-rating.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.place_of_supply_rules: For GST/HST purposes, supplies of intangible personal property (such as music licenses) are generally considered supplied in Canada if the recipient is a Canadian resident (except where the supply relates to real property or goods situated in Canada), and outside Canada if the recipient is a non-resident and the supply is not for use in Canada; the ULC must apply these rules to determine whether 5% GST applies or whether the supply may be zero-rated. For BC PST, a supply is subject to PST if the tangible personal property is delivered or brought into British Columbia for use in BC.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.cross_border_digital_services_obligation: Since July 1, 2021, Canada requires non-resident vendors and platform operators supplying digital products and services (including royalty-free music subscriptions) to Canadian resident consumers to register under the simplified GST/HST regime, collect 5% GST at the point of sale, and remit via CRA; marketplace facilitators such as online audio licensing platforms may be deemed the supplier for GST purposes where they control the payment processing and delivery, and the ULC must document who is the deemed supplier in its Stripe/PayPal arrangements. The ULC itself, as a Canadian resident supplier, must charge 5% GST on Canadian B2B and B2C sales unless the supply is zero-rated as an export.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.provincial_sales_tax_nexus: BC PST applies to retail sales, leases, or licensing of taxable tangible personal property and specified services in BC; digital audio files and streaming subscriptions are generally not taxable PST items, but if the ULC sells physical media (compact discs, flash drives, or other tangible carriers containing music) to BC consumers, 7% PST is payable by the purchaser and must be collected by the ULC under its PST vendor number. There is no BC digital services tax at present.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.gst_input_tax_credit_framework: The ULC may claim input tax credits for GST paid on Canadian purchases and expenses used in its commercial audio licensing business, subject to the general 90% or more commercial activity test and substantiation rules under section 169 of the Excise Tax Act; expenses related to zero-rated export sales remain creditable, and CRA Form GST60 applies to rebate requests for non-resident vendors.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.bad_debt_and_adjustment_notes: Credit notes and adjustments for cancelled subscriptions must be documented with GST/HST adjustment notes (Form GST20 for rebates); bad debts on Canadian taxable supplies may give rise to a GST/HST bad debt deduction under section 231 of the Excise Tax Act, provided the amount has been included in net tax and written off.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: The BC ULC may claim 0% GST on exports of stock music licenses, sound recordings, and related copyright rights where the supply qualifies as a zero-rated export of goods under Part I of Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act (physical media exported from Canada) or as a zero-rated supply of intangible personal property or services to a non-resident under Part V of Schedule VI (all or substantially all — 90% or more — of the value or use of the copyright license occurs outside Canada). The royalties and subscription fees from foreign customers (U.S. and international) are eligible for zero-rating on a self-assessed basis; no separate withdrawal is required. The ULC must be able to demonstrate, through contracts, customer records, and payment processor data, that the recipient is a non-resident and that the licensed music is not exploited in Canada. Domestic Canadian sales remain subject to 5% GST, and zero-rating cannot be claimed for Canadian customers.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Customs Export Declaration (Form B13A) — mandatory for physical media shipments exported from Canada and presented to the Canada Border Services Agency; not applicable to purely electronic delivery of digital audio files
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill — evidence of physical export voyage from Canada, showing consignee name/address outside Canada; not applicable where files are delivered through the license platform

Inward Remittance Certificate — SWIFT MT103 credit confirmation, bank remittance advice, or Stripe/PayPal settlement statements evidencing receipt of foreign currency proceeds within 180 days from invoice date

Executed license, subscription, or royalty-free music agreement — contains the foreign customer identification, governing law clause, and an express restriction that the audio may not be used or exploited in Canada

Customer and transaction audit trail — IP-geolocation logs, billing country, foreign tax identification number, persistent customer master data, and end-to-end Stripe/PayPal transaction reconciliation demonstrating the export nature of each zero-rated supply
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA applies heightened audit scrutiny to export zero-rating claims, particularly for digital and intangible supplies, and will require the full documentation bundle described above; where substantiation is deficient, CRA may reassess the supply as taxable at 5% GST and levy arrears interest, with a general GST/HST reassessment period of four years (section 298 of the Excise Tax Act) and an income tax reassessment period of three years, extended to six years for misrepresentation attributable to neglect, and without limit for fraud. Civil penalties include gross-negligence penalties of 50% of the understated income tax or falsely claimed GST rebate, plus false-statement penalties under the Excise Tax Act, and criminal prosecution under section 239 of the Income Tax Act and section 327 of the Excise Tax Act with fines and imprisonment up to five years. Claimed refunds can be clawed back with compound interest; in cases of fraudulent export zero-rating (forged bills of lading or fabricated non-resident entities), the ULC and its directors may be assessed personally under joint and several liability rules.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.refund_claim_procedure_for_non_residents: Non-resident purchasers of Canadian audio licenses may obtain refunds of GST through CRA Form GST189, while the ULC, as a Canadian resident exporter, claims input tax credits and net tax refunds on its regular GST/HST return (Form GST34). Refund claims must include all underlying contract and remittance documentation; CRA may hold the refund pending complete verification under its refund/assessment holdback powers.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.retention_and_evidentiary_requirements: Books and records supporting zero-rated export supplies must be retained for at least six years (seven years for corporate income tax purposes is recommended); records must be in English or French, or accompanied by an English/French translation; electronic records must be maintained in a CRA-readable format and reconciled to the GST/HST return and financial statements.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.customs_procedures_for_physical_media: If the ULC exports tangible carriers containing sound recordings, an approved exporter may clear goods using Form B13A, and the goods must be exported within the prescribed timeframe and proof of export must be kept; CBSA enforces export controls with penalties under the Customs Act and customs export declarations may be subject to verification, with failure resulting in administrative monetary penalties.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.transfer_pricing_and_treaty_consideratio: Cross-border royalty-free stock music licenses to U.S. customers involve royalties or sale proceeds that must be priced at arm's length under section 247 of the Income Tax Act; the Canada-U.S. Tax Convention protects Canadian-resident ULCs from U.S. permanent establishment risk where sales are conducted on a pure e-commerce basis, and foreign tax credits may be available for U.S. withholding taxes on certain streams, reduced through treaty provisions for royalties and business profits.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada); Foreign Exchange Administration: no dedicated exchange-control authority, with AML/ATF supervision exercised by FINTRAC and OSFI under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and the Bank Act.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible under a floating exchange-rate regime. Canada imposes no foreign-exchange controls on current or capital account transactions. Profit remittances and royalty distributions from a BC ULC are not subject to exchange-control approval; the only constraints are corporate solvency requirements under the Business Corporations Act (British Columbia), normal tax withholding obligations under the Income Tax Act (Canada), and anti-money-laundering due diligence.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory export-proceeds surrender requirement nor mandatory conversion ratio in Canada. Export receipts may be retained, repatriated, or converted freely. For royalty-free stock music licensing revenue generated by the BC ULC, receipts may be received in foreign currency and converted to CAD at the entity's discretion without mandated timeline or ratio.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Overseas digital Electronic Money Institutions and fintech payment platforms cannot operate as deposit-taking banks in Canada without a banking licence under the Bank Act. They may operate as Money Service Businesses (MSBs) or Foreign Money Service Businesses (FMSBs) only if registered with FINTRAC and compliant with Canadian AML/ATF obligations. Cross-border treasury viability is Low to Medium: acceptable for payment-rail integration with Stripe/PayPal and settlement of streaming royalties, but unsuitable for capital escrow, custody, or high-volume clearing without a Canadian Schedule I bank as the primary liquidity anchor.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Directors of a BC ULC are not statutorily required to appear physically at a bank branch; Canadian AML/KYC rules permit non-face-to-face account opening through remote identity verification, including electronic ID verification and video interviews. However, in practice major Canadian Schedule I banks may impose a physical presence or in-branch verification requirement for higher-risk structures, foreign-resident directors, or complex beneficial ownership chains. For a BC ULC with non-resident ownership, most banks will require at minimum a video interview with all directors and authorized signatories, plus certified corporate documents and a Canadian mailing or registered-office address.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unlimited Liability Corporation (ULC) structure with non-resident shareholders and unlimited liability status may trigger enhanced due diligence and beneficial-ownership review.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Dossier must include: certificate of incorporation and certificate of good standing from BC Registry; corporate register and minute book showing issuance of shares; register of directors and registered office; AMF/BC Beneficial Ownership Transparency Act declaration or equivalent; notarized copies of passport/ID for all directors and UBOs; explanation of unlimited liability and tax pass-through election; registered office address and operating agreement.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border royalty flows from platforms such as Stripe, PayPal, and music-licensing marketplaces may resemble intellectual-property monetization and require source-of-funds and source-of-wealth validation.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Dossier must include: master licensing agreements; royalty statements from digital content platforms; published pricing schedule for royalty-free stock music library; bank references from source jurisdictions; audited or management-prepared financial statements; tax residency certificates; and an AML risk assessment demonstrating the low-risk nature of the commercial audio licensing marketplace.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of interposed purpose entities or jurisdictions with high perceived ML/TF risk in the chain of payment routing for subscription proceeds.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Dossier must include: complete corporate ownership chart showing all intermediate holding entities; evidence of economic substance in British Columbia; affidavits from directors of ultimate beneficial owners; source of wire transfer and expected transaction volume; copy of the global cash-flow model; confirmation of no shell-company indicia; and legal opinion from Canadian counsel confirming purpose and tax discipline.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unusual transaction patterns such as rapid repatriation of royalty receipts or frequent same-day conversions to offshore accounts.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Dossier must include: treasury policy and FX risk-management mandate; monthly cash-flow forecast; tax distribution and dividend/resolution documentation; transfer pricing or intercompany royalty analysis; and transactional logs mapped to commercial contracts avoiding artificial fragmentation of receipts.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital contributions to the BC ULC are executed via SWIFT MT103 or domestic CAD wire through Canada's Lynx high-value payment system. The wire must identify the sending entity, the recipient ULC account, and the nature of payment using standard remittance information such as 'Contribution to share capital' or 'Equity injection'. Canada maintains no exchange-control permit; however, the bank may require proof of corporate authorization, a resolution of directors, and confirmation that filings under the Statistics Act (e.g., direct investment reporting to Statistics Canada) are assessed for reportable thresholds. The correspondent-clearing route is typically USD-cleared through a US intermediary bank, with final credit in CAD via the receiving Canadian bank; purpose codes for Canadian cross-border reporting are derived from the account statement, but no statutory purpose-code classification is mandatory for the remitter.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade settlements from the ULC's treasury accounts are executed through SWIFT MT103 for international wire payments, Lynx for high-value CAD payouts, and Commercial Letters of Credit for documentary trade where counterparty credit risk mitigation is required. For subscription-based royalty-free stock music licensing, recurring foreign payments to licensors, distributors, and technology vendors are normally cleared via ACH, EFT Credit, and platform payout rails integrated with Stripe and PayPal. Settlement instructions must include exact beneficiary legal names, IBAN or domestic account codes, SWIFT/BIC routing, and beneficiary bank details; supporting documents for FX and regulatory review include invoices, purchase orders, and licensing contracts.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright CAD/USD and CAD/EUR forward exchange contracts with Schedule I Canadian banks
Cross-currency swaps for CAD and USD/EUR cash-flow hedging
FX futures and cleared swaps listed on recognized Canadian exchanges or eligible derivatives markets

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 27% combined general corporate income tax rate: 15% federal plus 12% British Columbia provincial tax. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation may generally access an 11% combined small-business rate on eligible active business income within the applicable federal and British Columbia business limits. A British Columbia unlimited liability corporation is generally a taxable Canadian corporation and is not automatically tax-transparent under Canadian law.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: The federal small-business rate is generally 9%, and the British Columbia small-business rate is generally 2%, subject to eligibility, associated-corporation allocation, taxable-capital limitations, and business-limit rules. The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development regime may provide investment tax credits for qualifying research and development. The British Columbia Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit and other sector incentives generally do not apply automatically to audio licensing or stock-music activities. Canadian non-capital losses generally carry forward 20 taxation years and back 3 taxation years; net capital losses generally carry forward indefinitely and back 3 taxation years. Losses may be restricted on an acquisition of control or a change in business.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, including applicable schedules and financial statement information; filed electronically through CRA Corporation Internet Filing using approved tax software or through CRA-authorized representative access. British Columbia provincial corporate tax is generally administered through the federal T2 return. Form T2SCH5 is used for British Columbia provincial tax information where applicable. A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada generally files T2 under the Income Tax Act.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual. Corporate tax instalments are generally monthly, or quarterly for eligible corporations, but instalments do not replace the annual T2 return.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 return is due within 6 months after the corporation's taxation year-end. Any balance is generally due 2 months after year-end, or 3 months after year-end for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations meeting the statutory conditions. Instalment payments are generally due monthly on the last day of each month, with quarterly instalments available only where statutory eligibility conditions are met.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number, T2 program account, corporation type, taxation year start and end dates, province of permanent establishment, and principal business activity.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the corporation's Canadian legal name and BN. Identify British Columbia as the relevant permanent-establishment province if the corporation has a British Columbia permanent establishment. Report the actual taxation year, not the incorporation date unless they coincide.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Page 1, Corporation status and ownership
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Canadian-controlled private corporation status, public corporation status, other private corporation status, associated corporations, and control information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A ULC owned or controlled by non-residents will generally not be a CCPC. Review foreign ownership and control at the relevant time. Do not claim CCPC small-business treatment without satisfying the Canadian-control tests.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Page 1, Taxable income and tax payable
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income, federal tax, provincial or territorial tax, credits, instalments, refundable amounts, balance payable, or refund.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include income from Canadian business operations and other taxable Canadian-source amounts as required. A corporation carrying on business in Canada may be taxable on worldwide income subject to treaty allocation and foreign tax relief rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 1, Net income for tax purposes
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of accounting net income or loss to net income or loss for tax purposes, including non-deductible expenses, tax depreciation, reserves, provisions, and accounting adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reverse non-deductible expenses, including unsupported shareholder charges, accounting reserves, capital expenditures improperly expensed, and penalties. Reconcile foreign-currency amounts using an acceptable and consistently applied methodology.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax depreciation by class, additions, dispositions, undepreciated capital cost, recapture, terminal losses, and available incentives.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Classify Canadian business equipment, servers, production assets, and software-related capital expenditures under the applicable capital-cost allowance rules. Maintain acquisition invoices, use records, and disposition evidence.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal and provincial tax calculation, small-business deduction, general rate reduction, and other corporate tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Do not claim the small-business deduction merely because the entity is a ULC. Test Canadian control, active-business income, associated corporations, taxable capital, and specified investment-business exclusions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 23, Agreement among associated Canadian-controlled private corporations
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of the business limit among associated CCPCs where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Generally not applicable where the corporation is not a CCPC. Consider direct and indirect control, related persons, partnership interests, and option rights before concluding that no association exists.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 9, Connected corporations and associated corporations
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclosure of corporations connected with or associated with the filing corporation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose relevant Canadian and foreign relationships where required. Foreign ownership, common control, and ULC ownership chains require coordinated Canadian, United States, and treaty analysis.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Specified shareholder names, addresses, share classes, ownership percentages, and voting information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report non-resident shareholders and ownership accurately. Maintain beneficial ownership records, share registers, nominee arrangements, and changes during the year.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Revenue, cost of sales, operating expenses, financing expenses, depreciation, and net income based on the corporation's financial statements.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Separate licensing revenue, subscription revenue, platform commissions, advertising, refunds, payment-processing costs, and foreign exchange gains or losses. Reconcile Stripe and PayPal gross settlements to accounting revenue and fees.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: General Index of Financial Information balance-sheet and income-statement classifications.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use consistent GIFI codes and reconcile the GIFI statements to audited, review-engagement, or internal financial statements. Do not net payment-platform receivables against fees unless accounting standards permit it.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 11, Transactions with shareholders, directors, officers, and employees
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loans, advances, benefits, and other transactions involving shareholders, directors, officers, and employees.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose shareholder loans, personal expenses, management charges, and related-party benefits. Avoid undocumented debit balances and below-market arrangements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information relevant to a non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada or claiming treaty protection.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the applicable non-resident corporation disclosures and identify Canadian permanent-establishment facts. Treaty reliance does not eliminate filing obligations where the corporation carries on business in Canada unless the statutory and treaty conditions are satisfied.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T106 Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Transactions with non-arm's-length non-residents, including services, royalties, interest, financing, asset transfers, and intercompany balances.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File where the aggregate reportable transaction amount exceeds the applicable CAD 1 million threshold or where otherwise required. Report gross transaction amounts by category and counterparty, not merely year-end balances.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T1134 Information Return Relating to Controlled and Not-Controlled Foreign Affiliates
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign affiliate ownership, income, surplus, dividends, and related transactions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File if the Canadian corporation owns or is deemed to own reportable foreign affiliates. Determine whether foreign platform, IP, or operating subsidiaries are foreign affiliates before finalizing the T2.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of taxable income and provincial tax treatment based on permanent establishments and payroll or gross-revenue factors where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify all Canadian permanent establishments and allocate income under the applicable federal and provincial rules. A British Columbia registration alone does not prove that all income is attributable to British Columbia.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing generally attracts a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% of the unpaid balance for each complete month late, generally capped at 12 months. A repeat late filer may face a higher penalty. Interest accrues on unpaid tax, penalties, and instalment deficiencies at CRA prescribed rates, compounded daily. Failure to file required T106, T1134, or other information returns can create separate penalties, commonly CAD 25 per day subject to statutory minimums and maximums, with enhanced penalties for gross negligence or deliberate non-compliance.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on taxable dividends paid or credited by a Canadian corporation to a non-resident, subject to treaty reduction. Under the Canada-United States income tax treaty, the rate is generally 5% for a qualifying corporate shareholder beneficially owning at least 10% of the voting power and 15% in other cases, subject to treaty limitation-on-benefits and other conditions. Other treaties commonly provide rates between 5% and 15%, but the applicable treaty must be reviewed separately.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: Obtain and retain a valid Form NR301 declaration, or equivalent reliable documentary evidence, establishing the payee's name, address, residence for treaty purposes, beneficial ownership, and entitlement to treaty benefits. Confirm limitation-on-benefits, principal-purpose, anti-conduit, and beneficial-ownership requirements. The payer should apply the correct reduced rate at payment, remit Part XIII withholding to the CRA by the 15th day of the month following payment, and file the applicable T5 information return and recipient slip. If excessive withholding occurred, the non-resident generally claims a refund using Form NR7-R within the statutory period. A ULC's classification as fiscally transparent in another country does not automatically make it treaty-entitled in Canada.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: The domestic Part XIII rate is generally 25% on Canadian-source royalties and interest paid or credited to non-residents. Treaty rates vary by instrument and recipient; many Canadian treaties reduce copyright, software, or similar royalty withholding to approximately 10%, while some treaties provide exemptions or lower rates for arm's-length interest. Under the Canada-United States treaty, qualifying arm's-length interest is generally exempt from Canadian withholding, subject to exclusions such as participating or contingent interest and other specified categories; royalties commonly remain subject to a reduced treaty rate. Software, music, sound recordings, platform access, and content-license payments must be characterized by legal rights granted, not invoice labels. Related-party interest must satisfy transfer-pricing, thin-capitalization, withholding, and interest-limitation rules.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: For Canadian transfer-pricing documentation, contemporaneous records are required for non-arm's-length non-resident transactions under section 247 of the Income Tax Act. The T106 reporting threshold is generally CAD 1 million of aggregate reportable non-arm's-length non-resident transactions for the year. Canada has no universally applicable standalone statutory Local File or Master File threshold equivalent to jurisdictions that mandate both documents for all large groups. Large multinational enterprise groups may have Country-by-Country reporting obligations where consolidated group revenue meets the EUR 750 million threshold and the Canadian reporting conditions apply. CRA may require detailed local-file-style documentation regardless of transaction size where it is relevant to the audit.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no separate general Economic Substance Regulations regime equivalent to the United Arab Emirates, Cayman Islands, or certain other jurisdictions. Substance remains relevant under the transfer-pricing arm's-length principle, treaty beneficial-ownership analysis, permanent-establishment rules, the general anti-avoidance rule, specific anti-avoidance provisions, thin-capitalization rules, and principal-purpose or treaty-abuse doctrines. A Canadian ULC should maintain Canadian-directed governance, commercial decision-making, personnel or outsourced operational capacity, books and records, contractual control of licensed rights, risk management, and banking evidence consistent with its claimed functions and risks. A royalty-free or low-margin label does not justify zero compensation where the entity performs marketplace, marketing, localization, curation, customer-support, or IP-development functions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Tax Reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Concealing subscription or licensing revenue, omitting Stripe or PayPal receipts, fabricating expenses, backdating agreements, claiming personal expenditures as business costs, or knowingly making false T2, T106, T1134, GST/HST, or payroll filings.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Income Tax Act, tax evasion can result in prosecution, fines generally ranging from 50% to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded, imprisonment of up to 5 years, reassessment of tax, interest, gross-negligence penalties, and civil collection measures. False statements or omissions may attract penalties of 50% of the understated tax or improperly claimed credit, subject to statutory rules.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face criminal prosecution and imprisonment for knowing participation. Corporate status does not protect a director who personally commits, authorizes, acquiesces in, or directs the offence. Directors may also face derivative liability for unremitted source deductions and GST/HST, subject to statutory due-diligence defences.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Remit Non-Resident Withholding Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, royalties, interest, management fees, or other Part XIII amounts to non-residents without withholding, relying on an invalid treaty certificate, or failing to remit withheld tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The payer may be assessed for the unremitted amount, interest, and penalties. The standard failure-to-deduct or failure-to-remit penalty can be 10% of the amount required to be deducted or remitted, increasing to 20% for knowing or grossly negligent conduct. Repeated or deliberate failures may create additional penalties and prosecution exposure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be jointly and severally liable for unremitted source deductions, including Part XIII amounts, if the corporation failed to remit and statutory due-diligence requirements are not met. Personal assets may be pursued after corporate recovery steps.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying excessive royalties, management fees, interest, or platform charges to related non-residents, shifting Canadian profit through unsupported pricing, or failing to maintain contemporaneous records.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may reassess under section 247, deny or reduce deductions, adjust income, impose a transfer-pricing penalty generally equal to 10% of the adjustment where statutory conditions are met, and charge interest. Secondary withholding-tax, thin-capitalization, and treaty consequences may also arise.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may incur civil and criminal exposure where they knowingly participate in false records, fraud, or tax evasion. Ordinary transfer-pricing errors generally create corporate tax liability rather than automatic personal liability, but director liability can arise from wilful conduct or unremitted statutory amounts.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a nominal Canadian ULC with no genuine Canadian functions to obtain treaty benefits, routing dividends or royalties through conduit entities, misrepresenting beneficial ownership, or creating circular payment arrangements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Treaty benefits may be denied under beneficial-ownership, limitation-on-benefits, principal-purpose, anti-conduit, or Canadian general anti-avoidance rules. Assessments may include withholding tax, interest, penalties, and denial of deductions. CRA may challenge the arrangement based on legal rights, purpose, and factual substance.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly implement sham arrangements or false treaty claims may face civil penalties, prosecution, fines, and imprisonment. Corporate separateness will not shield personal fraudulent conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register where required, treating taxable Canadian supplies as exempt, misclassifying digital audio subscriptions, failing to collect GST/HST, or failing to reconcile gross payment-platform receipts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation may owe uncollected GST/HST, interest, late-filing and late-remittance penalties, and gross-negligence penalties. Certain digital-economy rules can apply based on supplier status, customer location, platform structure, and Canadian revenue thresholds.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for unremitted GST/HST where statutory director-liability conditions are met and due diligence is unavailable. Deliberate false invoicing or collection conduct may create criminal exposure.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Treating employees as contractors without analysis, failing to deduct CPP, EI, and income tax, paying undeclared director remuneration, or using foreign contractors to conceal Canadian employment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Assessments may include unremitted deductions, employer contributions, interest, penalties, and payroll information-return penalties. Misclassification may also generate employment-law and provincial workers' compensation exposure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be jointly and severally liable for unremitted payroll source deductions if statutory conditions are met. Criminal liability may arise for intentional falsification or obstruction.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Corporate Records and Beneficial Ownership Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining inaccurate registers, concealing beneficial owners, using nominee shareholders without proper records, failing to preserve accounting records, or issuing undocumented shareholder loans.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation may face corporate-law fines, tax reassessments, denial of deductions, penalties, audit escalation, and possible dissolution or administrative consequences depending on the governing federal or British Columbia statute.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face statutory fines, civil claims, fiduciary-duty liability, and prosecution where records are deliberately falsified or destroyed. Beneficial-ownership concealment can also trigger AML and proceeds-of-crime scrutiny.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Anti-Money Laundering and Proceeds of Crime
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Accepting suspicious funds, disguising source of funds through Stripe or PayPal, structuring transactions, ignoring sanctions indicators, or using the company to transfer proceeds of crime.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and Criminal Code can support compliance orders, administrative monetary penalties, seizure, forfeiture, prosecution, substantial fines, and imprisonment. Payment processors may suspend accounts and report suspicious activity.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face criminal fines, asset forfeiture, travel restrictions imposed through criminal or immigration processes, and imprisonment for knowing participation, facilitation, laundering, or sanctions evasion.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Copyright, Music Licensing, and Royalty Misrepresentation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Representing music as royalty-free without valid chain-of-title evidence, sublicensing tracks beyond the acquired rights, using unlicensed samples, or breaching territorial, platform, synchronization, or commercial-use restrictions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Rights holders may seek injunctions, statutory damages, actual damages, accounting of profits, delivery-up, and costs under the Copyright Act. Commercial infringement can also create criminal exposure in aggravated cases and can invalidate customer licenses.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for their own infringing acts, authorization, misrepresentation, or knowing participation. Corporate incorporation does not immunize personal copyright infringement or fraud.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Fraudulent Insolvency, Asset Stripping, and Improper Distributions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Distributing dividends while insolvent, extracting assets before tax liabilities are paid, transferring IP or cash to related parties for inadequate consideration, or using the ULC's unlimited liability structure to evade creditors.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Transactions may be set aside under corporate, insolvency, fraudulent-conveyance, or creditor-protection laws. Consequences may include repayment, damages, injunctions, director-officer liability, bankruptcy proceedings, and criminal fraud charges.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face personal repayment obligations, civil restitution, disqualification, asset seizure, travel restrictions, and imprisonment where conduct is fraudulent or criminal. An unlimited liability corporation may expose shareholders to additional liability under applicable corporate law.
